strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: neural operators can struggle on high-contrast multiscale PDEs, while GMsFEM is accurate but has an expensive offline basis-construction stage.

The core idea of predicting local GMsFEM basis subspaces, rather than directly predicting PDE solutions or individual basis functions, is well motivated. The subspace-alignment loss is a natural and appropriate way to handle sign and basis non-identifiability.
The experimental results show consistent improvements over a standalone FFNO solution predictor and substantial speedups over classical GMsFEM basis generation for the reported settings.
The paper is generally readable and includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including architecture search ranges, optimizers, training epochs, and compute hardware.

The method retains an attractive structural advantage over direct solution-predicting neural operators: once local basis subspaces are learned, the online solve can adapt to different right-hand sides and boundary conditions more naturally than a fixed operator trained for one forcing distribution.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for a top-tier acceptance threshold. Experiments are limited to two steady-state 2D PDE settings, structured grids, one coarse-grid configuration, relatively small 100x100 resolutions, and only 1000 coefficient samples. The claimed practicality for heterogeneous PDE simulation is therefore only partially supported.

The baseline suite is limited. The main learned baseline is a standalone FFNO, but the paper does not compare against stronger or more relevant alternatives such as force-conditioned neural operators, U-NO/modern FNO variants, DeepONet-style operator baselines, learned eigenspace surrogates, graph neural operators, or hybrid multiscale-learning methods beyond one cited related work.

The computational-efficiency claim is incomplete. The reported 50-60x speedup compares only per-instance basis generation time and appears to exclude the cost of generating GMsFEM supervision, training three neural operators, hyperparameter search, and amortization regimes. This makes the practical speedup claim hard to interpret.

The claim that GMsFEM-NO is independent of forcing terms is somewhat weakened by the experimental protocol: appendix tables report different selected hyperparameters for different forcing settings, and the paper does not clearly show a single trained basis model reused across all forcing distributions without retuning.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported, despite several claimed improvements being modest, especially versus classical GMsFEM. The authors acknowledge this, but it materially weakens the evidence.

The observation that the learned method sometimes outperforms the teacher GMsFEM basis is interesting but under-explained. Without theoretical analysis or deeper diagnostics, it is unclear whether this reflects useful regularization, hyperparameter differences, numerical artifacts, or evaluation variance.

The method lacks theoretical guarantees on stability, approximation quality, coercivity, or preservation of important finite-element structure when using predicted subspaces. For a hybrid numerical-method paper, this absence limits confidence outside the tested cases.

The Richards-equation setup is under-specified. It is not fully clear how nonlinear solves, basis construction, and dependence on the solution-dependent conductivity are handled, nor how general the learned bases are for different nonlinear regimes.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released code and data at submission time, and some dataset-generation details are not sufficient to independently reconstruct the exact coefficient fields and PDE solution pipeline.

The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: subspace losses and learned surrogates for expensive numerical components are established themes, and the paper would need broader empirical evidence or stronger analysis to clearly rise above a specialized hybrid implementation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in scientific machine learning: accelerating multiscale PDE solvers for high-contrast heterogeneous coefficients, where standard neural operators can struggle.

The central idea of predicting local GMsFEM basis subspaces rather than full PDE solutions is sensible and potentially useful, especially because the learned offline component is independent of the forcing term in principle.

The proposed subspace alignment loss is a natural fit for the non-identifiability of basis functions, and the experiments show that it improves over a sign-invariant L2 basis loss on the reported benchmarks.
The manuscript is mostly readable and includes implementation details for several hyperparameters, optimizers, architectures, and training protocols in the appendix.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited for a top-tier AI venue. The method is essentially a hybrid of established GMsFEM machinery, FFNOs, and a standard subspace/Grassmann-style alignment objective; the paper does not sufficiently position the loss or method against related reduced-basis, operator-learning, and learned multiscale-method literature.

The experimental scope is narrow. Results are shown only on 2D structured grids at 100x100 resolution, a 5x5 coarse grid, two steady-state PDE settings, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, and one apparent coefficient/data distribution. This is too limited to support broad claims about practical heterogeneous PDE simulation.

The comparison to standalone neural operators is not fully convincing. The standalone NO is evaluated mainly as a direct solution predictor, while the proposed method uses strong built-in numerical structure; this is useful, but the paper lacks comparisons to stronger hybrid or physics-informed baselines and does not establish that the chosen NO baseline is competitive.

The speedup claim is overstated. The reported 50-60x acceleration covers only basis-function generation and appears to exclude training cost, hyperparameter search, data generation, classical solves used to produce targets, matrix assembly/projection, and amortization analysis. For a practical solver claim, these costs matter.

The claim that GMsFEM-NO can outperform the GMsFEM basis it is trained on is surprising and insufficiently justified. The explanation that the NO learns a more efficient subspace is plausible but not supported by deeper analysis, theoretical argument, or diagnostics of the learned subspaces.

The out-of-distribution evidence is weak. The only OOD test concerns changing the forcing term for the standalone NO; because GMsFEM basis functions are expected to be independent of forcing, this comparison is somewhat structurally favorable. There is no substantial OOD evaluation over coefficient distributions, contrast levels, grid resolutions, boundary conditions, geometries, or PDE families.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. The authors explicitly report no error bars, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or seed variability, despite relying on small numerical differences in some tables, such as GMsFEM-NO being marginally better than GMsFEM.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The authors state that code and data will be released only upon acceptance, and important dataset-generation details, coefficient distribution specification, runtime accounting, and exact experimental scripts are not available in the submission.

The ablations are incomplete. The paper varies the loss, number of basis functions, and some architecture settings, but does not isolate the effects of learned subspace prediction versus simpler surrogate models, alternative subspace losses, direct prediction of local operators, coefficient-distribution shifts, coarse-grid size, or resolution scaling.

Overall significance is below the acceptance bar. The approach may be useful as an applied numerical surrogate, but the paper currently reads as an incremental and narrowly validated engineering combination rather than a strong AI contribution with convincing generality.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated hybrid of GMsFEM and neural operators: learning local multiscale basis subspaces rather than directly predicting PDE solutions or individual basis functions.
The subspace alignment loss is well motivated by the non-identifiability of basis functions and is empirically stronger than the sign-invariant L2 basis loss across both PDE settings.

The empirical results are encouraging: GMsFEM-NO improves over standalone NOs on high-contrast problems, remains naturally independent of the right-hand side, and gives large reported speedups for basis generation relative to classical GMsFEM offline construction.

The paper is mostly clear, with useful algorithmic description, comparisons across diffusion and Richards equations, ablations over loss functions, and appendix details for neural operator training hyperparameters.
The work addresses a meaningful problem for multiscale PDE solvers and offers a plausible path for combining numerical structure with learned acceleration.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still relatively narrow for a top-tier venue: only two steady-state PDE families, one structured-grid setting, fixed zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, and relatively small 100x100 grids are tested.

The main comparison set is limited. The paper compares against standalone FFNO and classical GMsFEM, but does not sufficiently compare to other learned multiscale, neural Galerkin, DeepONet/FNO variants, or prior neural-basis GMsFEM approaches beyond a brief discussion.

The computational speedup claim focuses on basis generation time and does not fully account for training cost, generation of GMsFEM supervision, hyperparameter search, total solve time, or scaling with dataset size and grid resolution.

The claim that the learned method can outperform the GMsFEM basis it is trained on is intriguing but underexplained; it would benefit from stronger analysis, repeated runs, and checks that the comparison is not due to tuning or evaluation artifacts.

There are no error bars or statistical significance estimates, and the authors explicitly acknowledge not running repeated trials, which weakens confidence in several relatively small performance differences.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code and data are not released, and some architectural details are scattered through many appendix tables rather than being presented as a compact, executable specification.

The stated generality to boundary conditions and forcing terms is only partially demonstrated. Independence from forcing is structurally plausible for the basis construction, but the empirical evidence covers only two forcing distributions and no boundary-condition variation.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated hybrid method: using neural operators to predict local GMsFEM basis subspaces, then retaining the GMsFEM coarse solve. This is a sensible way to combine learned acceleration with a numerically grounded solver structure.

The subspace alignment loss is well matched to the mathematical object being learned. It addresses sign and rotation ambiguity of eigenbasis functions more naturally than pointwise basis regression, and the empirical comparison against the adapted L2 loss supports this design choice.

The experiments are broader than many neural PDE papers: results cover 2D and 3D diffusion/Richards problems, multiple forcing terms, different grid resolutions, data efficiency, OOD forcing for standalone neural operators, and appendices with heat equation and mixed boundary condition extensions.

The method shows strong empirical speedups for basis generation and generally matches standard GMsFEM accuracy closely, while outperforming standalone neural operators on high-contrast and variable-forcing settings.
The comparison set includes several relevant baselines, including F-FNO, GNOT, Transolver++, POD-style methods, kernel methods, and DeepPOD, with some hyperparameter search details provided.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental. Learning local reduced bases/subspaces and combining neural models with multiscale or reduced-order methods is an active area, and the main new ingredient is largely the specific GMsFEM-NO formulation plus Grassmannian-style loss.

The theoretical support is weaker than the main text suggests. The appendix mostly derives the connection between the loss and projection/Grassmannian distance, but the claimed solution-error connection is informal and even notes that a more formal principal-angle-to-energy-error analysis remains future work.

The evaluation is still restricted to synthetic structured-grid permeability fields generated by a particular KLE distribution. The paper’s claims about robustness and large-scale practical simulation would be stronger with more diverse coefficient families, real porous-media data, irregular domains, or substantially larger-scale tests.

The computational-cost analysis is confusing and possibly flawed: the breakeven table reports negative breakeven sample counts, which is hard to interpret and seems inconsistent with the stated formula unless prior training-data generation is being accounted for in an unusual way. This weakens the efficiency claim despite the impressive per-instance speedups.

The comparison to standalone neural operators is partly favorable by construction because GMsFEM-NO is independent of the right-hand side while the standalone models learn solution maps tied to forcing. This is a valid advantage, but the paper should better separate architectural merit from problem-conditioning differences and compare against stronger conditioning strategies.

The method currently depends on structured grids and specialized separate models for local domain types. This limits generality, and the extension to irregular domains is only discussed as future work.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper says source code and optimal parameters will be released, but exact data-generation settings, trained model details, and solver implementation choices are not fully sufficient to independently reproduce all results from the manuscript alone.
Some presentation issues reduce confidence, including grammatical errors, typos in tables/figures, and occasional overclaiming such as saying the results 'prove' the method is fast and accurate.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing the expensive offline basis construction stage in GMsFEM for heterogeneous multiscale PDEs.
The proposed framing of learning local multiscale subspaces rather than direct PDE solutions is sensible and potentially useful for multi-query settings.
The empirical section covers several settings, including 2D and 3D diffusion/Richards equations, different forcing terms, and some extensions to heat equations and mixed boundary conditions.
The subspace alignment loss is a reasonable design choice and empirically improves over a sign-invariant basis-wise L2 loss.
weaknesses: The main novelty is limited. The SAL objective is essentially a standard principal-angle/Grassmannian subspace distance, and the paper does not establish a substantially new theoretical or algorithmic contribution beyond applying this to GMsFEM basis prediction.

The theoretical support is weak. The appendix contains an informal and incomplete error argument, acknowledges missing energy-norm analysis, and does not rigorously justify the central claim that subspace alignment ensures solver accuracy.

The computational efficiency claim is not convincingly supported. Training data generation requires running traditional GMsFEM, training costs are large, and the break-even analysis table appears internally inconsistent, with negative break-even values despite positive costs. This undermines the paper's strongest practical claim.

The comparison to standalone neural operators is partly unfair or under-specified. The OOD forcing-term experiment mainly shows that models trained for one fixed forcing do not generalize to another if the forcing is not part of the input, which is not a meaningful indictment of neural operators in general.

Baselines are not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. Several reduced-order/operator-learning baselines are relegated to the appendix, details are hard to assess, and there is no clear evidence that all baselines are implemented in their strongest or most comparable form.

The evaluation is narrow despite many tables: coefficients are synthetic KLE fields from a limited distribution, grids are structured, boundary-condition and time-dependent results are limited, and the 100^3 setting uses only 50 test samples.

The claimed discretization invariance is overstated. Training on 100 or 250 and testing on 500 shows noticeable degradation relative to GMsFEM, and the evidence is limited to closely related structured grids.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says source code and optimal parameters will be made public, but the submission itself does not provide enough detail to independently reproduce all results, especially the GMsFEM implementation and data-generation pipeline.
Some empirical claims are stronger than the results support. H1 errors can be substantially worse than L2 errors, and some extensions show degraded gradient accuracy even when L2 remains small.

Overall, the paper is technically plausible and has a useful engineering idea, but the novelty, theoretical grounding, fairness of evaluation, and amortized efficiency evidence are not strong enough for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically motivated hybridization of GMsFEM and neural operators: learning local multiscale basis subspaces rather than full PDE solution operators is a sensible way to preserve some structure of the numerical method while accelerating the expensive offline stage.

The empirical results are fairly broad for this problem class, covering 2D and 3D elliptic diffusion, nonlinear steady-state Richards equation, different forcing terms, reduced training data, higher-resolution evaluation, and additional appendix tests for heat equations and mixed boundary conditions.
The reported speedups for basis generation are substantial, especially in 3D, and the method appears to retain nearly the same solution accuracy as standard GMsFEM across the main benchmark tables.

The comparison to standalone neural operators is meaningful: the paper highlights an important advantage of the proposed basis-learning approach, namely independence from the PDE right-hand side and better robustness under forcing distribution shifts.

The subspace-alignment framing is appropriate for eigenbasis prediction, since individual eigenvectors have sign and rotation ambiguities; this is a more principled target than naive pointwise basis-function regression.
weaknesses: The main novelty is somewhat incremental: using neural networks to accelerate local basis construction in multiscale/reduced-order methods is a natural and related direction, and the paper should more sharply distinguish its contribution from prior neural basis, neural homogenization, LOD, and reduced-order modeling work.

The theoretical treatment of the loss is weak and partly overstated. The SAL loss is essentially a standard Grassmann/ projection-distance objective, and the justification for the SAL-PR term is not convincing: if the subspace is aligned, rotations within the subspace should not matter for the projection, so the claimed gap is mathematically unclear.

The evaluation is still limited to structured grids and synthetic KLE coefficient fields with fixed forms of heterogeneity. This leaves uncertainty about robustness on real geological media, irregular domains, unstructured meshes, or more diverse high-contrast coefficient families.

The computational story is incomplete. The headline speedups exclude the cost of generating training data and training several separate models; the breakeven table is helpful but confusingly formatted and should be clarified, including whether training data generation is parallelized, how many model trainings are required, and how performance scales with coarse-grid choices.

Reproducibility is only partial: the paper says code and optimal parameters will be made publicly available, but does not currently provide enough implementation detail to fully reproduce all results, particularly the PDE solvers, local eigenproblem construction, data generation choices, and baseline implementations.

Baseline comparisons are uneven. Strong standalone NO comparisons are mainly shown for 2D 250x250, while broader 3D comparisons and comparisons to modern geometry-aware or multiscale operator-learning methods are limited. Some appendix baselines appear weaker or evaluated under different settings.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, such as broad statements about reliability, resolution invariance, and large-scale applicability. The 500x500 transfer results are promising but still show a noticeable gap to GMsFEM, and the largest 3D setting uses only 150 training samples and 50 test samples.

The paper would benefit from more ablations on the number of basis functions, coarse-grid resolution, model-per-domain-type design, sensitivity to coefficient contrast, and failure modes when predicted bases are inaccurate or non-orthogonal.
